Virtual pH Sensor — Results Explorer

A GRU-based virtual pH sensor for hydroponic farming. Predict water pH from cheaper sensors so the fragile physical pH probe is used less and lasts longer. Based on Moniruzzaman et al., Alexandria Engineering Journal 143 (2026).

0.65

75.6%
Physical sensor usage cut

The story: we reproduced the paper (R²=0.98), discovered that number was inflated by data leakage, built an honest leakage-free test, fixed the GRU so it genuinely generalizes, and added a confidence system + fault-robustness that give the virtual sensor real value. Click any item on the left to see full details.

00_summary_card.png
📘 What problem are we solving? (plain English)
  • Hydroponics = growing plants in water instead of soil. The water must stay at the right pH (acidity) or plants suffer.
  • pH is measured with a physical probe dipped in the water. These probes are fragile: they wear out, drift, and need frequent replacing.
  • Our idea (a virtual sensor): train a model to predict pH from the other, cheaper, durable sensors (temperature, humidity, nutrient level, water level).
  • If the prediction is trustworthy, we can read the real probe far less often → it lasts much longer and costs less to maintain.
  • Technically this is time-series forecasting: use the last 10 minutes of sensor readings to predict the next minute's pH.
📘 How to read the scores (important for the review)
  • R² (R-squared, 0→1): the fraction of the pattern the model explains. 1 = perfect. It is NOT an accuracy percentage — never say 'R²=0.98 means 98% accurate'.
  • MAE (Mean Absolute Error): the average size of the mistake, in pH units. Lower = better. 0.02 means we're off by ~0.02 pH on average.
  • RMSE: like MAE but punishes big mistakes much harder. If RMSE is much bigger than MAE, a few large errors are dominating.
  • within ±0.05 pH: the % of predictions within 0.05 of the truth — this is the closest thing to an intuitive 'accuracy %'.
  • Data leakage: accidentally letting the model see answers it shouldn't during training. It makes scores look great but fake. This is the central finding of our project.

Concepts & glossary

Every term used in this project, explained simply.

📘 The models we used (10 total)
  • Persistence — the 'dumb' baseline: predict next pH = last pH. Every real model must beat this to be worth anything.
  • Linear Regression — fits a straight-line relationship. Simplest.
  • Random Forest / ExtraTrees — many decision trees averaged; strong, robust tree models.
  • XGBoost — gradient-boosted trees; a very popular, powerful ML model.
  • ARIMA — a classic statistics forecasting method (uses only past pH).
  • GRU / LSTM — 'recurrent' neural networks built for sequences; they remember recent history. GRU is the paper's main model.
  • Transformer — an attention-based model (the tech behind modern AI).
  • Improved GRU — our upgraded GRU (the 'delta head' version).
📘 Key techniques
  • Look-back window = 10: each prediction uses the previous 10 one-minute readings of all sensors.
  • Normalization (MinMax): squash every sensor to a 0–1 range so training is stable. We fit it on training data only (no leakage).
  • Train / Validation / Test split: train = learn; validation = tune settings; test = the final unseen exam.
  • Random split (leaky) vs Temporal split (honest): random shuffles windows so test overlaps train (cheating); temporal keeps a time gap so the test is a genuine future period.
  • Delta head: instead of predicting absolute pH, predict the change and add it to the last value. Stops the model from cheating by copying the last reading.
  • Huber loss: a training objective that ignores extreme outliers, so a couple of sensor glitches don't dominate.
  • MC-Dropout: run the model several times with a bit of randomness; if predictions wobble a lot, the model is uncertain.
  • ONNX: a portable model file format that runs on tiny edge devices like a Raspberry Pi.

What it means: the original GRU fails here (R²=0.03) — worse than the trivial "repeat last value" persistence baseline. Our Improved GRU recovers to R²≈0.65, matching the strongest models (ExtraTrees, persistence) while using half the parameters. R² is "fraction of variation explained" (1=perfect), NOT an accuracy %.
📘 Why this table is the one that matters
  • This uses the temporal (leakage-free) split: we train on the earlier period, leave a gap, and test on a genuinely future period the model has never seen.
  • That's how the sensor would really be used — predicting the future, not filling gaps between known points.
  • Because there's no leakage, these numbers are lower than the paper's 0.98 — but they are honest. Lower-but-honest beats higher-but-fake in any serious review.
📘 How to read each row
  • Persistence (R²=0.65) — the bar every model must clear. On this smooth 1-minute data, 'repeat the last value' is already strong because pH changes slowly.
  • Original GRU (R²=0.03) — collapses. It had memorised the leaky signal and can't forecast a real future window.
  • LSTM (0.17), Linear (0.19), RandomForest (0.26) — all weak here.
  • XGBoost (0.55), ExtraTrees (0.68) — the tree models generalise best; ExtraTrees is the single best model on the honest test.
  • Improved GRU (0.65) — our fix brings the GRU back up to match persistence and approach ExtraTrees, at less than half the parameters.
📘 The honest takeaway to say out loud

On clean data our Improved GRU ties the simple baselines rather than crushing them — because on a slow-moving signal, that's near the achievable ceiling. We say this openly. The GRU's real advantage is not this number; it's the confidence-based sensor switching and fault robustness (see the Novelty sections), which the simple baselines cannot provide.

Paper reproduction — random split

We reproduced the paper's R²=0.98 regime exactly.

ModelR²MAE (pH)RMSE (pH)within ±0.05 pH
GRU0.97990.01470.030498.1%
LSTM0.97940.01630.030898.7%
Persistence0.98150.00870.029297.5%
ExtraTrees0.98370.00760.027499.2%
XGBoost0.98340.00810.027699.2%
⚠ Important: even the trivial Persistence predictor reaches R²=0.98 here. That is the tell-tale sign of temporal data leakage — the score is inflated, not real skill. This is why we built the honest test.
📘 What exactly is the leakage here?
  • The 'random split' first cuts the data into 10-minute windows, then shuffles the windows into train/test.
  • Two neighbouring windows overlap by 9 of their 10 minutes and have almost-identical answers.
  • So a test window can be nearly the same as one the model trained on — the model has effectively already seen the answer.
  • Result: every model, even the dumb persistence one, scores ~0.98. The score measures memorisation, not forecasting ability.
📘 Did we do something wrong? No — we reproduced the paper faithfully

We first matched the paper's exact setup and got R²=0.9824 — proving our reproduction is correct. Then, auditing it, we found the leakage that this setup contains. Exposing that is a contribution, not a mistake. We keep this table only to show 'yes, we can reproduce the published number', then we move to the honest evaluation.

Improvement — original vs improved GRU

Same honest leakage-free test for both models.

MetricOriginal GRUImproved GRUChange
R²0.0300.650+0.62
MAE (pH)0.03900.0196−50%
RMSE (pH)0.04370.0263−40%
within ±0.05 pH72.3%94.4%+22 pts
Parameters24,05110,7332.24× smaller
What changed: the improved GRU predicts the change in pH (delta head) instead of the absolute value, plus Huber loss, dropout, weight decay, LR scheduler and early stopping. The delta head is the single change responsible for the jump.
📘 Why the 'delta head' is the key fix
  • The old GRU predicted the absolute pH. The easiest way to score well under leakage is to just echo the last value — so it never learned real structure and collapsed on the honest test.
  • The new GRU predicts the change (Δ) from the last pH, then adds it back: next pH = last pH + predicted change.
  • Now the network's only job is to learn the small deviation from 'stay the same' — which is exactly the useful signal.
  • Our ablation (Phase 5) proved it: every config with the delta head scored R²≈0.71 on validation; every config without it was near-zero or negative.
📘 The supporting techniques (each does one job)
  • Huber loss — stops 2 glitchy pH spikes from dominating training.
  • Dropout + weight decay — prevent over-fitting (memorising).
  • Learning-rate scheduler — automatically slows learning as it converges, for a cleaner final model.
  • Early stopping — stop when validation stops improving, keep the best model (not the last one).
  • Result: better accuracy AND a smaller model (10,733 vs 24,051 parameters) — 2.24× fewer knobs.
📘 How to read the loss curve below

The chart shows training loss and validation loss dropping over epochs. They fall together and flatten out — a sign of healthy learning with no over-fitting. Early stopping halts training once the validation loss stops improving.

Confidence-aware hybrid sensing

The model estimates its own uncertainty (MC-Dropout) and only calls the physical probe when unsure.

SystemPhysical readsR²MAE (pH)
Always physical (traditional)100%exact0
Pure virtual (no switching)0%0.6500.0196
Hybrid (confidence switching)24.4%0.6900.0163
75.6% fewer physical-probe reads
What it means: the hybrid system cut physical sensor usage by 75.6% while keeping accuracy — this is exactly the "extend sensor lifespan" goal, and it's measured, not assumed.
📘 How the model 'knows when it's unsure' (MC-Dropout)
  • Dropout normally randomly switches off parts of the network during training. We keep it ON at prediction time and run the model ~30 times on the same input.
  • If those 30 predictions agree → the model is confident. If they scatter → the model is unsure. The spread (std) is our uncertainty score.
  • The 'uncertainty vs error' chart below confirms this works: higher uncertainty really does line up with larger prediction errors.
📘 The switching policy (how it saves the probe)
  • Start in virtual mode — trust the model's prediction.
  • If uncertainty rises above a threshold, OR the tracked error drifts too high → switch to physical mode and read the real probe.
  • Thresholds were tuned on validation data (not the test), so the reported reduction is a fair estimate.
  • A slow 'safety cadence' still reads the probe occasionally even when confident, as a sanity check.
  • Net result: the probe is read only 24.4% of the time instead of 100% — a 75.6% reduction.
📘 Honest wording for the review

We report the measured reduction in probe reads (~76%). We do not claim a specific 'lifespan × N' number, because that needs a probe-wear model we didn't build. But since electrode wear grows with usage, far fewer reads is expected to meaningfully extend service life.

Robustness when the pH sensor fails

30% of the stream corrupted (missing, frozen, noisy, drifting, miscalibrated).

SystemR²MAE (pH)RMSE (pH)within ±0.05
Traditional (overall)-6.920.04310.124985.5%
Proposed (overall)0.890.00600.014498.3%
Traditional (during fault)-20.970.14390.228451.5%
Proposed (during fault)0.710.02020.026394.4%
What it means: a traditional system that trusts the broken probe collapses (R²=−6.9). The proposed system detects the fault and falls back to the virtual sensor, staying accurate (R²=0.89). This is a benefit persistence cannot provide.
📘 What faults did we simulate, and why?
  • Missing — the probe returns nothing (disconnected).
  • Dropout/frozen — the reading gets stuck at one value.
  • Noise — random jitter added to the reading.
  • Drift — a slowly growing bias (electrode ageing).
  • Calibration error — a constant offset (badly calibrated).
  • These are the five most common real ways a pH probe goes bad. We corrupt 30% of the test stream with them.
📘 Why the traditional system gets a NEGATIVE R²

R² can go below zero when a model is worse than just guessing the average. The traditional system blindly trusts the corrupted probe, so during faults it outputs badly wrong values — worse than a flat line. Our system detects the fault and switches to the virtual prediction, so it stays close to the truth (R²=0.89 overall, 0.71 even during the fault windows).

📘 Why this is the strongest argument for the project

On clean data, a simple predictor matches our model. But a simple predictor has no idea when the sensor is lying — it will happily pass on a frozen or miscalibrated reading. Our confidence + fallback design is what makes it a real, deployable safety feature. The chart below shows the green (proposed) line staying on the true pH while the red (traditional) line diverges in every shaded fault window.

Model efficiency & edge readiness

ModelParamsSize (.pt)Latency (mean)
GRU baseline24,05197.7 KB1.113 ms
Improved GRU10,73347.0 KB0.910 ms
ONNX export (Improved GRU): exported 6.8 KB, parity 0.0. Small and fast enough for a Raspberry Pi — sub-millisecond CPU inference and a ~7 KB portable model file.
📘 Why efficiency matters for this project
  • The whole point is to run on the edge — on a cheap device sitting by the hydroponic tank, not in the cloud.
  • Latency = how long one prediction takes. Ours is ~0.9 milliseconds on a plain CPU — effectively instant.
  • Parameters / size = how much memory it needs. 10,733 parameters and a ~7 KB ONNX file fit trivially on a Raspberry Pi.
  • ONNX is a universal model format. 'Parity 0.0' means the exported ONNX model gives identical outputs to the original PyTorch model — so nothing breaks when deployed.
  • Bonus: the improved model is smaller than the baseline (10,733 vs 24,051 params) yet more accurate on the honest test.

Largest-error analysis

Why is RMSE bigger than MAE?

A single worst prediction contributed ~49% of the total squared error, and the top-2 were physically-impossible one-step pH jumps (+0.83, +0.49) with no actuator active — uncaught sensor glitches. Removing just the worst 2 brings RMSE down to ≈0.017. We did not delete them; we used Huber loss to reduce their influence instead.
📘 Why does RMSE look worse than MAE?
  • MAE averages the mistakes normally. RMSE squares them first — so one big mistake counts enormously.
  • We found the single largest error alone caused ~49% of the total squared error. A handful of points were inflating RMSE.
  • Those points were +0.83 and +0.49 pH jumps in a single minute with no dosing happening — physically impossible, i.e. leftover sensor glitches, not model failures.
  • So the model is actually accurate (median error ≈0.011 pH); RMSE was just being dragged up by 1–2 bad data points.
📘 What we did about it (the honest, correct choice)

We did not quietly delete the awkward points to make numbers look better — that would be dishonest. Instead we switched to Huber loss, which naturally reduces the training influence of extreme outliers while keeping all the data. That's the principled fix.

Deep learning models — paper reproduction

The three neural networks from the paper, trained under identical settings (3 seeds, best run shown). Random split.

ModelR²MAE (pH)RMSE (pH)Params
GRU0.98240.01070.028524,051
LSTM0.98310.00920.027923,952
Transformer0.97030.02190.0369351,041
What it means: GRU and LSTM are essentially tied and both far more compact (~24k parameters) than the Transformer (~351k). The paper picks the GRU for its lower inference latency. Note: these are the random-split (leaky) numbers — see the honest comparison for the trustworthy ranking.
📘 What are GRU, LSTM and Transformer?
  • GRU and LSTM are 'recurrent' networks: they read the sequence one step at a time and carry a memory of what they've seen. Good for time-series. GRU is a simpler, faster LSTM.
  • Transformer uses 'attention' to look at all 10 time steps at once and weigh their importance. Powerful but much heavier here (351k parameters vs 24k).
  • Parameters = the model's tunable knobs. Fewer = smaller, faster, cheaper to run on small devices — which matters for a Raspberry-Pi deployment.
📘 Why the paper (and we) pick GRU

GRU and LSTM reach basically the same accuracy, but the GRU is compact and has lower inference latency, making it the best fit for a low-power edge device. The Transformer's extra size buys no accuracy here, so it's not worth it. The charts below compare all three: predictions vs truth, error distributions, and outlier counts.

ARIMA — classical statistical baseline

A traditional time-series model using only past pH. We grid-searched the (p,d,q) order by AIC and it selected (3,1,3) — the same order the paper reports.

VersionR²MAE (pH)RMSE (pH)AIC
Our ARIMA(3,1,3)0.7200.01790.0236-33084.0
Paper ARIMA(3,1,3)-1.960.1990.2237-63762.23
What it means: ARIMA only looks at past pH and cannot use the other sensors, so it is much weaker than the deep and tree models. This is exactly why a multivariate model is needed. (The paper reported a negative R² on their test window; on the smoother subset ours reaches R²≈0.72 — but still clearly the weakest approach.)
📘 What is ARIMA and what do (p,d,q) mean?
  • ARIMA = AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average — a classic statistical forecasting method from before deep learning.
  • p = how many past values it uses; d = how many times it differences the series to remove trends; q = how many past errors it corrects for.
  • We tried many (p,d,q) combinations and picked the best by AIC (a score balancing fit vs complexity). It chose (3,1,3) — the same as the paper, confirming our reproduction.
  • Its big limitation: it only sees past pH, not temperature, nutrients, etc. Since pH depends on those, ARIMA is fundamentally limited here — which motivates the multivariate GRU/tree models.

Classical machine-learning baselines

Non-deep learning models on the windowed features (the paper's Table 6 comparison).

ModelR²MAE (pH)RMSE (pH)MAPElatency (ms)
MLP0.97720.01450.03240.252%0.130
KNN0.97680.01270.03270.220%1.603
XGBoost0.98340.00810.02760.140%0.489
What it means: tree-based XGBoost is a very strong, fast baseline — a key reason we compared against it. On the honest leakage-free test, tree models (ExtraTrees/XGBoost) were among the best, which is why our final claim is honest rather than "the GRU beats everything."
📘 What are these three models?
  • MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) — a basic neural network with fully-connected layers; no memory of sequence order.
  • KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) — predicts by finding the most similar past situations and averaging their pH.
  • XGBoost — builds many small decision trees in sequence, each fixing the previous ones' mistakes; extremely strong on tabular data and very fast.
  • We feed them the flattened 10-minute window as input features.
📘 Why include them at all?

Good science compares a new model against strong, simple alternatives — not just weak ones. By testing XGBoost and the tree models, we can honestly answer 'is the GRU actually the best choice?' The answer on the honest split was nuanced (trees do very well too), which is why our final report is careful and truthful rather than over-claiming.

Which sensors relate to pH?

Pearson correlation of every sensor with pH.

Reproduces the paper's Figure 9. The exhaust fan has ≈0 correlation with pH; pH depends on several interdependent variables, which is why a multivariate model is used instead of a univariate one.
📘 What is a correlation heatmap?
  • Correlation measures how strongly two things move together, from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to +1 (move together).
  • Each coloured square shows the correlation between two sensors. Read the 'pH' row/column to see what relates to pH.
  • Sensors like temperature, TDS (nutrients) and humidity show real relationships with pH; the exhaust fan shows ≈0 (irrelevant).
  • Takeaway: no single sensor determines pH — several matter together — so a model that combines them all (multivariate) is the right choice.
